text.p: Australia's Labor opposition on Tuesday dismissed the government's 1997/98 budget as "directionless, shapeless and hopeless".
Opposition treasury spokesman Gareth Evans said the budget did nothing to fix high unemployment, provide help for struggling families or overturn the country's poor private savings level.
Opposition leader Kim Beazley stopped short of saying Labor would block key measures in the hostile Senate.
But he said the opposition would look seriously at measures such as the tax rebate on savings and increased prices for medicines.
"I look very closely at the new drugs (measure)," he told reporters. "I think that that's an area that requires the closest possible scrutiny."
Beazley said the savings rebate did not put enough money back into the pockets of voters and would not significantly boost national savings.
Evans said in a statement: "This budget fails the three big tests it had to pass."
Treasurer Peter Costello earlier announced his budget for the year from July, projecting a $3.85 billion underlying deficit -- excluding asset sales.
But the budget held out little hope for bringing down Australia's unemployment rate which was 8.7 perent in April. It forecast an 8.25 percent year average jobless rate in 1997/98.
Costello announced a 15 percent tax rebate for income earned on savings, but the amount being returned to voters was less than originally promised.

The Labor Party needs to muster the support of the minority Australian Democrats party in the Upper House, called the Senate, as well as the independents and the Greens to overturn or block government legislation. The Democrats said earlier that there was not too much in the budget that it would object to.
